title: Large uncommitted modifications make it impossible to use `aider` on a small file tracked in git
body:
Reproduction steps:
* Pick any git repo and run `aider smallfile`, where `smallfile` is already committed and there are no uncommitted changes - you should successfully end up at the prompt `smallfile>`
* Shut down aider
* Modify some file other than `smallfile` and add or remove a bunch of lines (enough changes that there will be too many tokens in the prompt)
* Run `aider smallfile` again - this time, you should see an error that looks like the following:
```
<large diff>
<big error message>
openai.error.InvalidRequestError: This model's maximum context length is 4097 tokens. However, your messages resulted in 9132 tokens. Please reduce the length of the messages.
```

Current workaround:
```
cp smallfile untrackedsmallfile
aider untrackedsmallfile
```
^and since it is not tracked, the diff is irrelevant. I think it would be nice if this was still possible if the file was tracked
e.g. if the diff is too large, forget about committing files that were not explicitly mentioned in the `aider` invocation

Feel free to close this issue if you do not feel like this is a priority. The current workaround is fine for me at the moment. And it is simple enough to just make sure not to have uncommitted changes before running `aider`

title: Feature Request: Easier CTAGS execution on specific file extension
body:
Hey there, 
So I want to become a product manager, and want to understand codebases better with the help of aider.

For this I would like to do things less manual and more automated.
Here is what I thought about - and asked GPT-4 based on your README:
```
I want to run aider with the ctags on all .py files in a different repo, how do I do this?

```
And the answer was:
```
To run Aider with ctags on all .py files in a different repo, follow these steps:

Open your terminal and navigate to the root directory of the target repository.
cd /path/to/your/repo
Install the universal ctags if you haven’t already:
# For Ubuntu/Debian-based systems
sudo apt-get install universal-ctags

# For macOS (using Homebrew)
brew install --HEAD universal-ctags/universal-ctags/universal-ctags
Generate the tags file for your repo using ctags:
ctags -R *.py
This command will recursively search for all .py files and generate a tags file in the repository root.

Run Aider with the --ctags flag and specify all .py files you want to work on:
aider --ctags file1.py file2.py ...
Replace file1.py, file2.py, etc., with the paths to the source code files you want to work on.

Now, Aider will launch using ctags for better understanding and modification of your codebase while working on specified .py files. If you don’t want to specify each individual .py file, you can use wildcards or other tools like [find](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/find.1.html) to pass all desired .py files as arguments.
```

And then I asked further - and received this:
```
You can accomplish this using the find command along with a wildcard to specify all .py files. Here’s an example of how you can do this:

Open your terminal or command prompt.
Navigate to the directory containing the .py files you want to work with.
Use the following command to pass all .py files as arguments to a script called your_script.py:
python your_script.py $(find . -name "*.py")
In this example, find . -name "*.py" will search for all .py files in the current directory and its subdirectories. The $( ... ) syntax will pass the output of the find command (i.e., the list of found .py files) as arguments

title: Feature Request: Support git worktrees
body:
I think git worktrees offer a great workflow for a tool like aider. Worktrees reduce the friction that naturally stems from having an external tool commit automatically, resulting in a smoother experience.

 In case you're not familiar: [man git-worktree](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree).


A sample workflow would look something like this:

```bash
mkdir mydir && cd mydir

# create a dummy repo
mkdir myrepo && cd myrepo && touch README.md && git init && git add -A && git commit -m "Initial commit"

# aider works here
aider -v

# create a worktree to fix some bug. CD into it.
mkdir ../worktrees
git worktree add ../worktrees/bugfix
cd ../worktrees/bugfix

# use aider to help fix the bug (This will result in the error shown below)
aider -v

title: Feature Request: support for regex/glob expressions in the `/add` function
body:
**Feature Description**
Currently, the `/add` function accepts directory paths to add the entire directory  or spefic file paths to the program's context. A useful enhancement would be to support the use of regex or glob expressions with the `/add` function. This would give users more flexibility and control to specify exactly which files to include.

**Proposed Solution**
Allow the `/add` function to interpret glob or regex patterns. For example, a user could use `/add src/*.py` to include only Python files from the `src` directory or `/add src/[A-C]*` to add only files that start with A, B, or C.

**Expected Behavior**
When a user runs `/add` with a regex or glob pattern, the program should add to the context only the files that match the pattern. The program should handle non-matching files or non-existent paths gracefully, preferably by ignoring them and printing a warning message.

**Alternatives Considered**
An alternative could be providing an additional function, say `/addPattern`, that accepts regex/glob patterns. This approach would leave the existing `/add` functionality unchanged for users who don't need the enhanced functionality.

**Additional Context**
Adding this feature would boost the flexibility of the `/add` function, making the program more convenient to use for a variety of tasks. Users could, for instance, exclude certain types of files or select a subset of files based on their naming conventions.

title: Feature Request: Automatic File & Context Window Access Management
body:
The quality of output and autonomy of Aider is excellent, however, the main limitation of autonomy is the requirement for the user to manage Aiders access to files and to ensure the context window size is not overwhelmed. If the management of file access and managing of the context window was offloaded to the AI to manage, it shouldn't need much, if any, input from the user to complete tasks.

I'm not sure if this is possible, but it could potentially achieve this if it was able to:
1. Autonomously check and manage the current amount of used tokens and take actions based on this check.
2. Analyse if any files can be dropped safely. 
3. Have an option to add files without a user accepting the request.
4. Trim non-relevant chat history.
5. Chunk large files so it can access a single function in a large file instead of the entire file.
Hopefully, with these capabilities, it could complete even longer tasks without any input from the user.

This is the first autonomous agent system that we've successfully been able to incorporate into our team's workflows so thanks very much to the creators and contributors!

title: feature request: support conventional commit messages
body:
Conventional commit messages are defined [here](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/#summary)

Aider can be compatible with conventional commits while still keeping the information currently in the commit messages.

Using conventional commits means other tooling that checks for conventional commits and uses these to generate for example changelogs, detect changes for semantic versioning and other things, do not need to understand the "unconventional" commit structure.

Conventional commit does not *explicitly* forbid the aider commits, but the typical suggestion is to use types that pass for example commitlint:

 https://github.com/conventional-changelog/commitlint/tree/master/%40commitlint/config-conventional

title: Does aider work with Bard, Claude or local LLM like gpt4all? Thanks!
Support for other LLMs, local LLMs, etc
body:
*This issue is a catch all for questions about using aider with other or local LLMs. The text below is taken from the [FAQ](https://aider.chat/docs/faq.html#can-i-use-aider-with-other-llms-local-llms-etc).*

Aider provides experimental support for LLMs other than OpenAI's GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. The support is currently only experimental for two reasons:

- GPT-3.5 is just barely capable of *editing code* to provide aider's interactive "pair programming" style workflow. None of the other models seem to be as capable as GPT-3.5 yet.
- Just "hooking up" aider to a new model by connecting to its API is almost certainly not enough to get it working in a useful way. Getting aider working well with GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 was a significant undertaking, involving [specific code editing prompts and backends for each model and extensive benchmarking](https://aider.chat/docs/benchmarks.html). Officially supporting each new LLM will probably require a similar effort to tailor the prompts and editing backends.

Numerous users have done experiments with numerous models. None of these experiments have yet identified other models that look like they are capable of working well with aider.

Once we see signs that a *particular* model is capable of code editing, it would be reasonable for aider to attempt to officially support such a model. Until then, aider will simply maintain experimental support for using alternative models.

### More information

For more information on connecting to other models, local models and Azure models please see the [FAQ](https://aider.chat/docs/faq.html#can-i-use-aider-with-other-llms-local-llms-etc).

There are ongoing discussions about [LLM integrations in the aider discord](https://discord.com/channels/1131200896827654144/1133060780649087048).

Here are some [GitHub issues which may contain relevant information](https://github.com/paul-gauthier/aider/issues?q=is%3Aissue+%23172).

title: Thoughts on internal architecture
body:
I've been looking at at some of the aider tickets like #170 and #172 and thought it was worth a conversation before trying to tackle them. I figure a little internal refactoring might make it a bunch easier to implement but didn't want to spend time on significant changes without discussion first.

It seems to me there might be some benefit of building up some internal concepts of 
- transport : how aider talks to the LLM (e.g. openai, text-generation-interface)
- model : which model you're talking to
- coder : which coder is driving the model (editblock, wholefile etc.)

It would then be straightforward to reference a setup as `openai.gpt-4-8k.editblock` and have a lot of information about what is going on.

For example for #170 we can keep using the openai transport layer as openrouter supports the interface but as we play with the claude (and other) models it would be nice to be able to easily switch out editblock vs wholefile coders to measure the performance.

For #172 I would be keen to experiment with a [text-generation-interface](https://github.com/huggingface/text-generation-inference) transport as we can have more control (and maybe less complexity?) than using an openAI api wrapper like fastchat or text-generation-webui. I'm also thinking we would likely need to write some specific coders to get any useful work out of the smaller open models.

I think this would also get us a long way to a simple plugin architecture where if we document what a transport or coder need to implement it becomes possible to incorporate 3rd party code with flags like --transport or --coder pointing to stand alone directories. I don't know if we would need or want a full blown plugin system but giving people the ability to easily implement their own transports, coders, (and maybe even commands?) might go a long way to keeping the core of aider lean and focused on the essentials.

Thoughts?

title: Only commit dirty files if GPT tries to edit them
body:
> I may end up moving the whole commit system to only committing the files which have been added to the chat. It's not ideal, because GPT could base its changes on other repo files which are dirty which never actually get commited by the user in their current state.

I wonder about a strategy of 
- check status of each file ChatGPT wants to update
- complain if any are dirty or not in git and require user intervention - maybe give the user the options to 
a) add/commit before changing 
b) change anyway 
c) abort

that would mean we could ditch the whole dirty check on startup which takes a while to get used to and give users more flexibility overall

If you add so much code to the aider chat that it exceeds the context window, OpenAI will return a "maximum content length" error immediately on each request. Aider could check the size of the request before sending it, and return a local error if the request is larger than the context window. This would avoid having those useless tokens counted against the rate limit.

title: Config file location should follow "modern" specifications
body:
Writing dotfiles into the root of user's home dir is not really a thing anymore.

For linux, there's the XDG base directory specification. This would make the location by default something like `~/.config/aider/config.yml`.  See https://gist.github.com/roalcantara/107ba66dfa3b9d023ac9329e639bc58c#file-xdg-cheat-sheet-md

On a mac `~/.config` is probably better for a terminal app than going to the "correct" `~/Library/Application Support/aider/config.yaml`. Tools like git, github copilot, gh cli, shells, neovim and many others use it or at least will make a symlink from there to Library.

On windows `%APPDATA%\Aider\config.yaml` is probably good.

body:
Example usage:
```
/test-command npm run test
/test-run
/test-fix
/test-first on
```

It's been found that [CodeT and Reflexion dramatically improve](https://twitter.com/johnjnay/status/1639362071807549446)  GPT-4's coding ability.  The idea would be to automatically run tests after every codegen and to retry codegen on an error.  GPT Engineer uses a similar strategy, I think.   Example workflow:

1. Before doing a batch of work, user calls /test-command <cmd> and /test-first on.
2. User Enters a prompt
3. Aider checks if a test method exists for the change, and if not generates it.
4. Aider attempts to make the code change for the prompt
5. Aider runs test command.
6. If an error occurred, create a prompt from the error output to attempt to fix the code.  Test again.
7. If an error occurred again, loop back to step 4 up to 10 times.   Reset the change.  Increase temperature.
8. After final failure, AI evaluates all error messages to find the least bad solution and apply its code change with an error notification. 

/test-command <command> also runs the test to make sure there weren't any preexisting failing tests.

Full Reflexion requires a vector database for long term memory, so perhaps that's too much for this ticket.

title: Proposal: Horizontally-Scalable LLM Requests
body:
# The Problem

Currently, `aider` appears to have a single-threaded approach to handling LLM requests and responses. This has been enough to make aider operate well at a basic level, but it limits what we can do if we're willing to spend more compute to solve our problems.

When we ask aider to do a programming task, we can potentially trigger many LLM requests, some of which could execute concurrently:

- Create a high-level plan based on the user's query
- Review the plan and make improvements
- Search the codebase for relevant files
- Come up with file management operations such as adding new files, removing files, or moving files
- Execute unit tests or build steps in order to validate code changes
  - Feed the validation results back into the LLM for feedback
  - Repeat until valid

# Proposal: Asynchronous LLM Requests

## 1. Put LLM requests into async functions

The first step is to make our LLM completion queries async.

## 2. Implement limits and checks to manage concurrency

LLMs are expensive to run. Some users will have higher or lower compute budgets.

We can keep this concurrency under control by using queues and workers. Because our workers are simply making HTTP requests, we do not need threads --asyncio is enough. I suggest that we have a queue of LLM requests, and a fixed number of workers.

For instance, if we have an API with a strict limit of 1 request per 10 seconds, we could spawn just one worker and have it sleep for 10 seconds, grab a work item from the queue, and repeat.

If, on the other hand, we have our own GPU cluster running llama with a private openai-compatible API, then we might want to run 8 workers each of which could make 5 requests per second.

### 2.a. Budgeting

Although we have managed the API-side requirements such as rate limiting, we may still incur higher costs than the user intends to budget for a given task.

To solve this, we could use a feature where we ask for a budget when `aider` receives a new high level instruction from the user. Each time a worker processes an LLM task from the queue, the associated cost would be accounted for. In conjunction with this, we would want some kind of cost estimation function and a way to scale the computational intensity that the `aider` agent applies to the task.

Costs could be "scaled down" by using fewer workers, doing fewer review passes, and disabling non-critical computationally-expensive processing steps for that query.

The goal would be to have `aider` output quality scale based on the budget of the user.

# Caveats

## Rate Limiting

Some providers have strict rate limits on API requests. We don't want to make more requests than our allowed quota.

Handled by #2 above.

## Costs and Budgeting

Costs could spiral out of control.

Handled by #2 above.

title: Proposal: HIL (Human in the Loop) Planning
body:
# The Problem

`aider` can do an impressively good job on its own, but like all current LLM-based agent systems, it often falls short. Many times, just like with human software developers, the problem can be caught and fixed early --in the planning stage.

# Proposed Solution

To solve this problem, we can apply a HIL (Human in the Loop) strategy to the planning phase of the `aider` agent. Here's what I believe the agent should do:

1. Accept user query
2. Have a brief conversation with the user to nail down requirements
3. Generate a plan
4. Have at least one automatic review pass of the plan (https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11366)
5. Propose plan to user
6. Iterate on the plan based on user feedback
7. Now it's time to continue with the regular `aider` agent coding process.

# Caveats

## Don't Annoy Users

For some users, or some specific tasks, we'll want `aider` to jump in and get right to coding. Therefore, we should have a CLI flag to `aider` to enable/disable this feature, and possibly even have an input for how much we want `aider` to get feedback from the user.

# Conclusion

There are some tasks where I certainly would not mind `aider` interviewing me, and getting my feedback on the plan before continuing. Just like with most human endeavors, if we put a little more thought and energy into the planning part of the process, we can get drastically better results and avoid major pitfalls before they have a chance to occur.

title: Better diffs
body:
Hey!

First off, great work on aider. It's inspiring and very useful! I was actually working on a fork of it for voice-to-code and then you released exactly that!

The one issue I'm having is just how slow the updates can be, primarily because aider writes out the whole file in the left side of the diff. 

I've noticed that if we're only updating one function, aider usually writes a diff on just that function. However, if you are writing anything in the highest scope of the file, like defining a new function or class, then the whole file gets updated in the diff. 

I think that if aider knows where it's going to put a new function in a file, that it should just write a few lines before where the edit is being inserted. This could be accomplished by explicitly saying which lines are being replaced in the diff, or you could determine a relative offset by matching line hashes. 

Happy to PR a solution on this if you wouldn't mind thinking it over and telling me how you'd like to approach it.

title: Custom instructions
body:
I have noticed a few issues (such as #248 #243 ) where people want specific behavior that might not be general enough to warrant a new feature and it's made me think about giving folks the ability to append instructions to the system prompt - similar to custom instructions in ChatGPT.

This could be a new flag in the config so set on a global, per project, or per run basis and would greatly increase the ability for people to customise aider. It might also help the folks interested in #172 get better performance out of different models without having to create and maintain lots of different system prompts.

It would be pretty easy to add in but my main concerns are
* messing with the system prompt could degrade aider's performance for people, so it would be possible for people to do thing
* it would make support harder - we'd now need version, model, and custom instructions as well as the description of the behaviour to understand what is going on.

What do folks think, worthwhile feature?

title: Force models to return JSON instead of free-form text
body:
Hi,

I have been experimenting with `aider` for the past few days and have been impressed. I have a local [HuggingFace TGI](https://github.com/huggingface/text-generation-inference) installation running Code Llama and a [LiteLLM wrapper](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/providers/huggingface#text-generation-interface-tgi---llms) that makes it compatible with OpenAI API. 

However, it is a little harder to make it follow the various prompts for editing, creating new files, etc. defined in the `aider` repo. The Code Llama model response often has a preamble and appendix of explanatory text such as, _"Sure, here's a new Python file that prints hello world..."_.

Is it possible to instead return JSON with specified keys and values so that it is easier to parse the LLM output? A lot of API services/frameworks have the ability to provide custom grammar/regex which are nothing but custom `LogitProcessor`s that bias logits so that the model response conforms to the grammar. For example, recently Llama.cpp added [grammar-based sampling](https://twitter.com/ggerganov/status/1698359882234142776?s=20).

OpenAI models are already very good at following instructions and returning JSON outputs due to their superior RLHF training. In the light of this, can we have force the models to return JSON responses instead of free-form text?

Thanks for the great work!

title: Consider switching from GitPython to another package
body:
GitPython doesn't support git repos with index version newer than v2. 

https://github.com/gitpython-developers/GitPython/issues/1075

Newer versions of git can create indexes with v3 and v4:

https://git-scm.com/docs/index-format

You can work around this problem by downgrading the index format of your repo:

```
git update-index --index-version=2 
```

But it would be nice if aider used a git package that supported new index formats.

It's worth noting that dulwich currently supports v3 but not v4:

https://github.com/jelmer/dulwich/blob/master/dulwich/index.py#L309C3-L309C3

title: Enhancement: Consider fuzzy matching of the SEARCH pattern.
body:
Hi!

Aider is an excellent tool, and as agentic software becomes more prevalent, I find that its shortfalls become more and more irritating. In a similar way that every computer is a slow horrible mess once you've used something better. 

With Aider, this is that the SEARCH block doesn't seem to match sometimes, and I might have waited minutes for the output of the conversation only to have no changes. I work-around this by doing small, focused increments as much as possible, but there is always a time where the change is just a little bit bigger, or GPT decides that the diff should be lengthy. My thought was a fuzzy matching on SEARCH patterns. I can't say that you aren't already doing this because I have not looked at the way Aider works in regard to file updates. But I suspect that the SEARCH pattern must be exact, down to the whitespace.

I'd like to open the discussion for ways Aider could, without harming the accuracy of the updates too much, improve this. Handling whitespace differently comes to mind, as does fuzzy matching (Levenshtein distance?).

title: User-defined aliases
body:
Hi, thanks for the great project! I was thinking it would be useful to have some sort of configuration for user-defined aliases at different scopes. 

For example, a user might define global aliases on their machine like: 
- `!` to be an alias for `/run` (https://github.com/paul-gauthier/aider/issues/334)

And then for projects we could commit in common aliases for development: 
- Adding files related to a section of the codebase, e.g. `/add_${feature}` as an alias for `/add $feature_source_file $other_file $another_related_file`
- Common run commands, e.g. `/clippy` as an alias for `/run cargo clippy -- -D warnings`

Aliases could be put under the same prefix as commands currently (like `/!` or `/clippy`) or under a different prefix to reduce confusion / collisions when new commands are released (maybe `!` and `!clippy`?).

title: Enhance Git Integration for Global .gitignore and Optional Suggestions [Feature Request]
body:
**Description:**
Users of "aider," often encounter situations where it suggests adding `.aider*` entries to my project's `.gitignore` files. While this is helpful, it can sometimes lead to redundancy and clutter in multiple repositories. To improve user experience and offer better control over Git integration, I propose the following enhancements:

**How to utlize gitignore global configs**

Example:
```
echo '.aider*' >> ~/.gitignore_global
git config --global core.excludesfile ~/.gitignore_global
```

Quote with other possible paths:

> $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/git/ignore, $GIT_DIR/info/exclude, .gitignore

from https://git-scm.com/docs/gitignore

> git config --get core.excludesfile

from https://stackoverflow.com/a/22885996/544721

1. **Global .gitignore Configuration:**
   - Allow users to specify a global `.gitignore` file that "aider" will utilize to determine which files should be globally ignored across all projects. This will help maintain cleaner and more consistent `.gitignore` files.
   - How it works with Git:
     - Users set a global `.gitignore` file path, e.g., `~/.gitignore_global`, using a command like:
       ```
       git config --global core.excludesfile ~/.gitignore_global
       ```
     - Git will automatically apply the rules from the global `.gitignore` file to all repositories, ensuring that files matching these patterns are ignored without needing to edit project-specific `.gitignore` files.

2. **Optional Flag: `--gitignore-aider-globally`:**
   - Introduce a new command-line flag (`--gitignore-aider-globally`) in "aider" to allow users to specify whether they want `.aider*` entries added to the project's `.gitignore` or rely on the global configuration.

**Expected Git Behavior:**
- Users can configure a global `.gitignore` file to centrally manage which files are ignored by Git across all repositories.
- Git will apply rules from the global `.gitignore` file to all repositories, ensuring consistent ignoring of specified files.
- Users have the option to control whether "aider" should suggest adding `.aider*` entries to the project's `.gitignore` file or utilize the global configuration with the `--gitignore-aider-globally` flag.

**Benefits:**
- Streamlined and consistent management of ignored files across multiple repositories.
- Improved user control and flexibility in handling `.aider*` entries in project-specific `.gitignore` files.
- Minimized repetition and clutter in `.gitignore` files.

**Additional Information:**
- These enhancements will provide a more seamless integration between "aider" and Git, making it easier for users to manage ignored files globally and per-project while maintaining a clean and organized Git repository structure.

title: Feature Request: AI-Enhanced Rebases
body:
## Motivation
I have been learning that it's best to do changes in very small chunks, (For instance update an interface, then modify its implementations one-by-one.
This leaves me with tons and tons of tiny commit messages, each with a bunch of useful information.

## Solution
What would be incredible is if we could issue a /squash command, where Aider passes these commits (and diffs of source code?) and a prompt off requesting they all be summarized and combined so that once a feature is complete, it has a clean and wonderful single commit.

There are existing tools that do GPT-powered commit messages, so we could probably take some inspiration from there.

I'd be happy to put in a PR if this is a feature you would be interested in, though I'd like to discuss how it should fit into the existing architecture.

title: Achronological (and possibly redundant) elements in the prompt when making the first request
body:
Consider the following scenario. I have a project with a single file `hello.py`, and I ask aider to make a change.
The language model invocations look like this:

```
system: backstory, examples, rules
user: here is the repo map, if you want to change something ask to make the files read-write, I'm not sharing any read-write files yet
assistant: ok
system: rules again
user: please do <what I ask>
(model completion) assistant: make hello.py read-write
```

```
system: backstory, examples, rules
user: here are the read-write files: hello.py content
assistant: ok
system: rules again
user: please do <what I ask>
assistant: make hello.py read-write
user: done
(model completion) assistant: <actual search-replace block>
```

Note that this is inconsistent, the file was already read-write in the story when the (simulated) assistant asked to make it read-write and the (simulated) user ageed.

Maybe this conversation could be skipped entirely. If not, maybe the content of the file should follow the read-write request:
```
...
assistant: make hello.py read-write
user: done
user: here are the read-write files: hello.py content
...
```

For comparison, when doing the second request, the ordering of messages is consistent:
```
system: backstory, examples, rules
user: please do <what I ask 1>
assistant: make hello.py read-write
user: done
assistant: <actual search-replace block 1>
user: updated
assistant: ok
user: here are the read-write files: hello.py content
assistant: ok
system: rules again
user: please do <what I ask 2>
(model completion) assistant: <actual search-replace block 2>
```

We can start with aider off the shelf now, then later use the data to train our own fine tuned model and use that for improved responses. 

I guess the dataset could be fine tuned to produce the new structured diff format... thoughts? 

Feel free to delete or close, as I'm not sure if this is within the scope of this project, but I felt the community may be struggling with the same thing.

I came into following wonderings.
There are cases when one wants Aider to not modify some sections of file, and is fine with others.
It can be either due to organisational reasons (this part of code I wrote, other part wrote someone else...),
or due to files structure. Regarding second case , my strong use case is having Unit Tests in same file , e.g. in Rust it's common to have unit tests section at the end of file. And let's assume in TDD style we have tests that define expectations about behaviour, and code failing. We don't want Aider to change tests section, only rest of the file.

What would be best way to approach it?

Yes, I understand that probably it's use case to use aider via programming library, still, few options coming to my mind...

title: [Workflow] fzf file selection
body:
Hey, love aider, just want to share the shell function I use for file selection using `fzf`, in case it's useful for anyone. 
Not sure if this could/should be implemented into the main program, but it can save some time when making file selections across larger code bases. 

Prerequisite is having `fzf` installed ( https://github.com/junegunn/fzf?tab=readme-ov-file#installation ).

The script allows for fuzzy finding files across a folder and its subfolders, while allowing directory and file exclusions to be specified to ignore at the top of the script. It also reads `.aiderignore` but this check is not robust and could be improved, as directories are only handled correctly if they're specified with a trailing slash (e.g. 'test/').

Files can be fuzzy-searched and selected using 'Tab' key, once confirmed with 'Enter' the selection is passed to `aider` (or just 'Enter' for a single file). The function is written to both work in Bash and ZSH.

![2024-03-03_14-26](https://github.com/paul-gauthier/aider/assets/4933693/a8618ad8-477a-43a1-b0f5-8a0883590fb2)

```
faider() {
    local dir_exclusions=('.git' '__pycache__' 'node_modules')
    local file_exclusions=('.aider*' '__init__.py' '*.log')
    local find_args=()
    local selected_files

    # Add directory exclusions
    for dir_exclusion in "${dir_exclusions[@]}"; do
        find_args+=(! -path "*/$dir_exclusion/*")
    done

    # Add file exclusions
    for file_exclusion in "${file_exclusions[@]}"; do
        find_args+=(! -name "$file_exclusion")
    done

    # Add exclusions from .aiderignore if it exists
    if [ -f ".aiderignore" ]; then
        while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n $line ]]; do
            # Skip empty lines and comments
            [[ $line = \#* ]] || [[ -z $line ]] && continue
            # Check if the line ends with a '/'
            if [[ $line == */ ]]; then
                # Remove the trailing '/' for directory exclusion
                local dir=${line%/}
                find_args+=(! -path "*/$dir/*")
            else
                find_args+=(! -name "$line")
            fi
        done < .aiderignore
    fi

    # Run find command and select files with fzf
    if [[ -n $ZSH_VERSION ]]; then
        # Zsh specific command
        selected_files=("${(@f)$(find . -type f "${find_args[@]}" -print | fzf --multi --exit-0)}")
    else
        # Bash specific command
        IFS=$'\n' read -d '' -r -a selected_files < <(find . -type f "${find_args[@]}" -print | fzf --multi --exit-0)
    fi

    # Check if any files were selected
    if [ -n "$selected_files" ]; then
        aider "${selected_files[@]}"
    else
        echo "No files selected."
    fi
}
```

title: Enhance error message for missing API Key
body:
### Feature Request: Improved Error Handling for Missing API Key

#### Current Behavior
Currently, if the OPENAI_API_KEY is not provided, the system currently throws a slightly confusing error message:
```
... (several traceback lines)
return text.replace(args.openai_api_key, "***")
TypeError: replace() argument 1 must be str, not None
```

This error message does not clearly indicate that the root cause is a missing API key, which can be confusing for users trying to troubleshoot their setup.

#### Proposed Change
It would be beneficial for usability if the error message could explicitly state that the OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable is missing, rather than indicating a type error with the `replace` method. A more descriptive error message could look something like this:
```
Error: Missing OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable. Please ensure you have set a valid OPENAI_API_KEY before running aider.
```

I don't have much experience making pull requests, but I could implement raising a ValueError with an informative message if args.openai_api_key is None. 
Thank you for this tool!

title: Add files based on content
body:
When refactoring a large codebase, it is hard to know exactly which files are needed and will be impacted by the refactoring. As a result, one generally has to spend time looking at the code and searching which files should be added to aider in a text editor before starting the refactoring.

For instance: if I want to ask aider to refactor the function `exampleFunction` (rename, change call parameters, etc.), I need to list all the files where that function appears and manually add them to aider.

One solution to make this workflow easier would be to allow the `/add` command (or a new command) to search for a specific string or pattern inside all the files in the current folder and all its sub-folders, and then automatically add the files where the string or patterns appear at least once.

Example: `/add-pattern exampleFunction`

    > Carlos E. Jimenez, John Yang, Alexander Wettig, Shunyu Yao, Kexin Pei, Ofir Press, Karthik Narasimhan
    > Language models have outpaced our ability to evaluate them effectively, but for their future development it is essential to study the frontier of their capabilities. We consider real-world software engineering to be a rich, sustainable, and challenging testbed for evaluating the next generation of language models. We therefore introduce SWE-bench, an evaluation framework including 2,294 software engineering problems drawn from real GitHub issues and corresponding pull requests across 12 popular Python repositories. Given a codebase along with a description of an issue to be resolved, a language model is tasked with editing the codebase to address the issue. Resolving issues in SWE-bench frequently requires understanding and coordinating changes across multiple functions, classes, and even files simultaneously, calling for models to interact with execution environments, process extremely long contexts and perform complex reasoning that goes far beyond traditional code generation. Our evaluations show that both state-of-the-art proprietary models and our fine-tuned model SWE-Llama can resolve only the simplest issues. Claude 2 and GPT-4 solve a mere 4.8% and 1.7% of instances respectively, even when provided with an oracle retriever. title: Explore whether stack graphs may be useful in this tool
body:
I'm not sure if this would add anything substantially different/better than the existing `tree-sitter` implementation, but I spent some time recently looking into stack graphs + related tooling, and I'm wondering if there may be benefits to this project to look at using `tree-sitter-graph` and/or the `stack-graphs` project (eg. `tree-sitter-stack-graphs-javascript`, etc); rather than just plain `tree-sitter`.

A few notes/links/references I recently collated RE: stack graphs + related libs:

> Stack Graphs (an evolution of Scope Graphs) sound like they could be really interesting/useful with regards to code navigation, symbol mapping, etc. Perhaps we could use them for module identification, or variable/function identifier naming stabilisation or similar?
> 
> - https://github.blog/changelog/2024-03-14-precise-code-navigation-for-typescript-projects/
>   - > Precise code navigation is now available for all TypeScript repositories.
>     > Precise code navigation gives more accurate results by only considering the set of classes, functions, and imported definitions that are visible at a given point in your code.
>     > 
>     > Precise code navigation is powered by the stack graphs framework.
>     > You can read about how [we use stack graphs for code navigation](https://github.blog/2021-12-09-introducing-stack-graphs/) and visit the [stack graphs definition for TypeScript](https://github.com/github/stack-graphs/tree/main/languages/tree-sitter-stack-graphs-typescript) to learn more.
>     - https://github.blog/2021-12-09-introducing-stack-graphs/
>       - > Introducing stack graphs
>       - > Precise code navigation is powered by stack graphs, a new open source framework we’ve created that lets you define the name binding rules for a programming language using a declarative, domain-specific language (DSL). With stack graphs, we can generate code navigation data for a repository without requiring any configuration from the repository owner, and without tapping into a build process or other CI job.
>       - LOTS of interesting stuff in this post..
>       - > As part of developing stack graphs, we’ve added a new graph construction language to Tree-sitter, which lets you construct arbitrary graph structures (including but not limited to stack graphs) from parsed CSTs. You use stanzas to define the gadget of graph nodes and edges that should be created for each occurrence of a Tree-sitter query, and how the newly created nodes and edges should connect to graph content that you’ve already created elsewhere.
>         - https://github.com/tree-sitter/tree-sitter-graph
>           - > `tree-sitter-graph`
>             > The tree-sitter-graph library defines a DSL for constructing arbitrary graph structures from source code that has been parsed using tree-sitter.

>             - > `tree-sitter-graph` support for VS Code
>               > This language extension for VS Code provides syntax support for `tree-sitter-graph` files.

>         >

>         - https://github.com/github/stack-graphs
>           - > Stack graphs
>             > The crates in this repository provide a Rust implementation of stack graphs, which allow you to define the name resolution rules for an arbitrary programming language in a way that is efficient, incremental, and does not need to tap into existing build or program analysis tools.
>           - https://docs.rs/stack-graphs/latest/stack_graphs/
>           - https://github.com/github/stack-graphs/tree/main/languages
>             - > This directory contains stack graphs definitions for specific languages.
>             - https://github.com/github/stack-graphs/tree/main/languages/tree-sitter-stack-graphs-javascript
>               - > `tree-sitter-stack-graphs` definition for JavaScript
>                 > This project defines `tree-sitter-stack-graphs` rules for JavaScript using the `tree-sitter-javascript` grammar.
>               - > The command-line program for `tree-sitter-stack-graphs-javascript` lets you do stack graph based analysis and lookup from the command line.
>                 - `cargo install --features cli tree-sitter-stack-graphs-javascript`
>                 - `tree-sitter-stack-graphs-javascript index SOURCE_DIR`
>                 - `tree-sitter-stack-graphs-javascript status SOURCE_DIR`
>                 - `tree-sitter-stack-graphs-javascript query definition SOURCE_PATH:LINE:COLUMN`
>             - https://github.com/github/stack-graphs/tree/main/languages/tree-sitter-stack-graphs-typescript
>               - > `tree-sitter-stack-graphs` definition for TypeScript
>                 > This project defines `tree-sitter-stack-graphs` rules for TypeScript using the `tree-sitter-typescript` grammar.
>               - > The command-line program for `tree-sitter-stack-graphs-typescript` lets you do stack graph based analysis and lookup from the command line.
>         - https://dcreager.net/talks/2021-strange-loop/
>           - Redirects to https://dcreager.net/talks/stack-graphs/
>           - > Incremental, zero-config Code Navigation using stack graphs.
>           - > In this talk I’ll describe stack graphs, which use a graphical notation to define the name binding rules for a programming language. They work equally well for dynamic languages like Python and JavaScript, and for static languages like Go and Java. Our solution is fast — processing most commits within seconds of us receiving your push. It does not require setting up a CI job, or tapping into a project-specific build process. And it is open-source, building on the tree-sitter project’s existing ecosystem of language tools.
>           - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=l2R1PTGcwrE
>             - > "Incremental, zero-config Code Nav using stack graphs" by Douglas Creager
>           - https://media.dcreager.net/dcreager-strange-loop-2021-slides.pdf

>     > - Search-based - searches all definitions and references across a repository to find entities with a given name
>     > - Precise - resolves definitions and references based on the set of classes, functions, and imported definitions at a given point in your code
>     >
>     > To learn more about these approaches, see "[Precise and search-based navigation](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/working-with-files/using-files/navigating-code-on-github#precise-and-search-based-navigation)."
>     - https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/working-with-files/using-files/navigating-code-on-github#precise-and-search-based-navigation
>       - > Precise and search-based navigation

title: Multiple Conversation Threads, Prompt Customization, and Conversation Templates
body:
Another feature that could enhance the flexibility and organization of using Aider in complex or multi-faceted projects is the support for multiple conversation threads.

Feature Request:

Please add support for multiple conversation threads in Aider, enabling users to maintain separate discussions or sessions on different aspects of the same repository without interference. This feature could be managed through a --thread command line parameter, which defaults to "main" but can be set to other names to switch between independent conversation histories and file selections.

Use Case:

In projects where different components or features require distinct but simultaneous development focus, having the ability to switch contexts within the same repository environment can be invaluable. For example, one might want to discuss database issues in one thread and UI enhancements in another, without mixing the conversations and relevant file edits.

Proposed Implementation:

Introduce a --thread parameter that specifies the active conversation thread.

Store conversation-specific data like .aider.input.history and other session files in thread-specific subdirectories or encode the thread name in the file names. For instance, using an .alder directory at the top level for global configurations, and thread-XXX subdirectories for each conversation thread's data, could help keep project directories organized and avoid clutter, while enabling future extensibility and per-thread customization.

Questions for Consideration:

Version Control for .alder Files: Is it considered good practice to check in .alder files into the repo to maintain conversation history across different development environments? What are the implications for privacy and clutter in version control, and uses of pre-configured thread templates for particular tasks like chatting about documentation, apis, porting, internationalization, etc. 

Customizing Prompts per Conversation: Beyond simply including files with instructions, is there a mechanism to customize or augment the built-in AI prompts based on the conversation thread? This could tailor the assistance more closely to the context of each thread. Could there be an /instruct command like /add that adds those files as system prompts instead of user input? 

Saved conversation threads could be used as Conversation Templates that are pre-configured, parameterized, and start private conversation threads that may or may not be ignored and checked into source code control. 

Conversation Templates could included pre-configured sets of files, wildcards, or dynamic procedural selections (like dependencies on .h files from selections of .c files, so a conversation about documentation could include all the header files, and a conversation about user interface could include all of the header files and all of the user interface .c files, and user interface api documentation). 

Selecting files per thread could be partially accomplished by threads having their own .alderignore files (including white lists) layered on top of the global repo wide alder white list. But procedure file selection by running shell commands or scripts would also be powerful. Also save and restore named sets of selected files on a per-conversation basis. So three layers of file name globbing + ignoring: repo, conversation thread, named file list. 

This enhancement would not only make it easier to manage multiple development streams within a single repository but also align Aider with more complex development workflows where multitasking across different components is necessary.

I would also love a "/foreach [list of files] [instructions]" command whose behavior could be specialized in each conversation. 

Thank you for considering this feature. I believe it could significantly enhance the practicality of Aider in more complex projects. I look forward to your insights and hopefully seeing this capability in a future release!

I am excited about the potential for this feature and how it could improve Aider!

title: gpt-4-turbo refactoring benchmark questions
body:
After reading https://aider.chat/2024/04/09/gpt-4-turbo.html I was wondering if there is a way to improve the new model's score in the 
refactoring benchmark. I executed a small number of the tests and they all failed. But not in a way I had expected (i.e. "# rest of the code remains unchanged"). They all failed in the same way. I created this minimal testcase to reproduce the failure:

Given a class that looks like this:
```
class MyClass:
    def f1(self):
        self.x = self.f2()
        self.y = self.f3()
    
    def f2(self):
        return 1

    def f3(self):
        return 2
```
gpt-4-turbo would generate a valid diff that results in this code:
```
class MyClass:
    def f1(self):
        self.x = f2()
        self.y = self.f3()
    
def f2(self):
    return 1

    def f3(self):
        return 2
```
It simply out indents f2, ignoring the fact that now f3 no longer belongs to MyClass. 
If the model is given the code and the task without aider's prompt, it generate the correct code from which I concluded that the model understands the task, but is unable to express it in the udiff format.

I then  gave the model a diff generate by another model, that produces the correct output, and asked it to revise the prompt. It did (basically it simplified aider's prompt) and with the new prompt gpt-4-turbo was able to correctly solve the minimal test case. But it still failed on the larger cases. The simplified prompt in coders/udiff_prompts.py was:
```
system_reminder = """# File editing rules:
    
Return edits similar to unified diffs that `diff -U0` would produce, including:
- The first 2 lines with the file paths without timestamps.
- Start each hunk of changes with `@@ ... @@`.
- Mark all lines that need to be removed or changed with`-`and all new or modified lines with`+`.
- Indentation matters in the diffs.
- Start a new hunk for each section of the file that needs changes.
- Output hunks in whatever order makes the most sense.
- When editing a function, method, loop, etc., use a hunk to replace the entire code block.
- To move code within a file, use 2 hunks: one to delete it from its current location, one to insert it in the new location.
- To make a new file, show a diff from `--- /dev/null` to `+++ path/to/new/file.ext`.
"""
```

My questions:
1) Did you publish the raw benchmark results somewhere? If no, would you consider it? I'd like to look at more of the failures and check what the causes are.
2) Assuming a large part of the failures are caused by the problem described above, do you think it's worthwhile to explore different prompts to "fix" these failures? Maybe you already have some idea what prompting technique to try to make the model better understand the udiff format.

title: Allow the user to optionally edit the output of /run before sending it to the model
body:
Hi,

I was thinking about stuff and [yesterday you told me being rather against adding a budget cutoff](https://github.com/paul-gauthier/aider/issues/257#issuecomment-2061759434) which I completely respect but that got me thinking about the /run function:

> /run <command>: Run a shell command and optionally add the output to the chat.


To me I can imagine situations where I really don't want to have a /run command get stuck in a while loop and output instantly 50k tokens of a nonsense warning for example. That might be costly for nothing and I don't know what steps aider has put in place to avoid that. Especially if there's no budget limit.

So I'm humbly speaking aloud a few ideas (maybe some of them are already implemented, I don't know!):
1. the output of /run should be smartly deduplicated. i.e. if you have 10 lines in a row with the same warning, print the first and last and `(...)` in between. That might save a lot of tokens
2. If the number of token is above a certain threshold, ask the user if the llm should be given stderr or stdout
3. Ability to keep only the last n lines/tokens of the output i.e. usually the error message)
4. Ability to edit the output before sending it to the LLM. For example this could be used to add context like "as soon as I approach the moue from the right corner, it crashes like that"

I hope this is useful and appreciated, I have yet to really test aider because I'm so afraid of unexpected costs!

body:
# The problem
When I ask Aider to commit my code changes (made outside using nvim), it response a typical git workflow.
```
> ok, could you commit current code (which contains my code change)?

As an AI language model, I don't have the capability to directly commit code to a git repository. However, I can help you prepare the code for a commit. If you have made changes to the set-diff.rkt file and you want to commit those

 1 Stage the changes for commit:

    git add set-diff.rkt

 2 Commit the changes with a message:

    git commit -m "Implement set difference functionality in set-diff.rkt"

Please execute these commands in your terminal or use your preferred Git GUI to commit the changes. If you need further assistance with the commit message or any other part of the process, feel free to ask!

title: Let aider grok and configure the environment and run commands autonomously
body:
### Issue

Aider is great. But it could be much better. For example, letting it to install tjings, run things, configure the environment and the projects directly. Currently it requires our intervention for 90% of those actions. Aider always asks the user to run this, run that. But isn’t it just a bunch of commands? It should be able to run them autonomously.  Just ask confirmation before running them.
What about letting Aider to examine the environment, the configuration files in every directory and subdirectory (.env, .bashrc, .zshrc, .jslint, requirements.txt, .toml, .gitignore, .cfg, .ini, etc.) and letting it to handle the configurations, the dependencies and the installed tools?. Once it understands the current configuration, it can also separate the projects and the sub projects in a folder, so that (for example) it won't mix pyprojects.toml files anymore when it edits them. (Many times I’ve found the .toml configurations of a project from a sub folder being copied to another subfolder ‘pyproject.toml’). 
Once aider groks the environment, it can also be able to understand if it is running in a docker, in a sandbox, in a devbox or in a github/microsoft workspace, etc. So it would finally stop trying to fix with the wrong configuration files in project/workspace/ instead of those in ~/. He must be able to access and understand dot files from the true root parent folder outside the project/workspace folder, so that he can correctly change the various configurations and permissions. Atbthe moment it doesn’t seem to understand what the right configurations file are or where it can find them. Aider needs more than a map of the git repo.. it needs a map of the entire dev environment.
Configurations files ARE part of the code after all, and when in dev mode they must be taken in consideration by Aider every time he makes changes to the source of the project. 
For example: "change my linter for JavaScript from eslint to jshint" or "extend the Python max line length to 120 characters in the riff configuration" or "migrate from Antigen to Antidote" or "install yarn-audit-fix and add it to my git hooks" or "add @parcel/diagnostic to the tests to run on this project" or "automatically add and commit to git all source files that pass the pytests," or "separate those two folders in two different pip projects", or "create the necessary boilerplate to make this script a complete pip package with tests/hooks/CI/github-scripts/logs/docs, etc. and publish it on github and pypi."
Maybe this would require to write some functions calling scripts to make easier for Aider to interact with the environment, but the alternative, since you cannot stop aider from trying to change things outside of the code, is to let it make a mess. My proposed solution is to make aider grok the environment he works in along with the projects configurations to enable it to making changes in a safe way with the help of some solid function calling scripts. As projects grow bigger and get more complex, aider ends up becoming a danger since it modifies so many things at the same time that it is easy to let some major errors or misconfigurations slip in undetected until it is too late.

Hey, first of all thanks for your wonderful project!

I've noticed that the default setup of Aider is at 926 MB now. This is mostly due to dependencies. Here's top 15:

```

15M     google
13M     grpc
```

The way around that is to make some dependencies optional. One low-hanging fruit is Streamlit, which is 484 MB (incluing its own dependencies)! To do that, you could [declare it as an extra](https://setuptools.pypa.io/en/latest/userguide/dependency_management.html#optional-dependencies):

```py
setup(
    name="aider",
    ...,
    extras_require={
        "browser": ["streamlit", "pyarrow", "pandas", ...],
    },
)
```

And check if it's available in the runtime:

```py
def launch_gui(args):
    from aider import gui
    try:
        from streamlit.web import cli
    except ModuleNotFoundError:
        print(
            "Aider was installed without web support. To add it, run:\n"
            "    pip install aider-chat[browser]"
        )
        sys.exit(1)
```

title: Feature Request:  Review Mode with Checklist for Aider
body:
**Context:**
When I ask Aider to review my code, it often identifies issues and suggests corrections. While some of these corrections are accurate, others are based on design choices that do not need to be changed. Currently, Aider goes ahead and implements all suggested changes and commits them, which sometimes results in unnecessary modifications that I need to undo, leading to diminishing returns.

**Request:**
I propose adding a "Review Mode" switch in the Aider browser interface, with an accompanying checklist feature. This mode would allow users to control how Aider behaves when reviewing code. In Review Mode, Aider would:

1. Identify and list potential issues and suggestions.
2. Provide a clear distinction between critical issues and those that might be intentional design choices.
3. Present a checklist of identified issues, allowing users to selectively check off the items they want to be fixed.
4. Allow users to selectively apply changes based on the review feedback.
5. Provide an option for users to add new issues to the checklist during the review process.

**Workflow:**
1. **Review Identification:** Aider scans the code and lists potential issues and suggestions.
2. **User Interaction:** Users review the checklist, check off the items they want to be addressed, and have the option to add new issues.
3. **Selective Fixes:** Aider only applies fixes to the checked items, respecting the user's design choices.
4. **Iterative Review:** Users can choose to re-evaluate the checklist after initial fixes to address more items if necessary.


**Benefits:**

- Enhanced user control over code changes.
- Reduced need to undo unnecessary modifications.
- Clearer understanding of the rationale behind design choices.
- More efficient and collaborative code review process.

Implementing this feature would streamline the code review process, ensuring that changes made by Aider align more closely with the user's intentions and providing a more interactive and user-friendly experience.

title: Add config option to prefix commit messages with Aider
body:
### Issue

First of all fantastic tool! I've been using it for 2 days and i'm already in love!

By default right now aider writes `<Your Name> (aider)` as the commit author for any commits it makes. Instead of (or in addition to) this i'd prefer if it wrote `Aider:` into the commit message. E.g.

```git
commit 4eb896bcf75ec7ea8c23c4c28553f5f888d37174
Author: Evan Thomas <evanrthom@gmail.com>
Date:   Wed Jun 26 18:35:09 2024 -0700

    Aider: <some commit message>
```

I prefer this because my workflow with aider involves a lot of git diffing and commit squashing. 
1. I ask aider to do something 
2. Review the changes by doing a `git difftool` of all recent commits 
3. Optionally make some small changes myself and go back to step 2
4. Either "accept the changes" by squashing them all and marking the author as me, or "reject" by resetting hard to the last non-aider commit

In order to do this it's useful to be able to see at a glance which commits are Aider's and which commits are mine. I find it much easier to distinguish between Aider's commits and mine if `Aider: ` is in the commit message than if it's in the author field.

Furthermore, when I squash it's convenient for me to change the commit message body in the process of doing an interactive rebase.  It's much less convenient for me to change the author, as that involves executing another git command after the squash. By carelessness I end up with a lot of commits with  `Author: Evan Thomas (aider)` even after step 4, and then it's hard to tell which commit's i've "Accepted" vs "Rejected". This mistake would be much harder to make if `Aider: ` was in the body

If you agree with the philosophy of this change i'm happy to try my hand at putting up a pr. Thanks again for the fantastic tool!

I'm experimenting with programming just by telling the AI what to change. When I use aider iteratively in this way and it doesn't quite work, I might end up making lots of commits. To see where I got to so far, I typically prepare a command like `git diff <last good commit> HEAD` and ask for changes based on what bit of code to move where, or describing what the result misses, etc., and then I squash them all.

Here's a sample of what that might look like:
```
Removed unnecessary code for calculating drag offset and simplified the drag event handling.
Improved the map marker dragging functionality by using the Google Maps API's projection methods to accurately calculate the new marker position during drag events.
Implemented drag and drop functionality for the map marker, updating its position based on the user's drag actions.

I would find the tool more useful for this workflow if my own prompts were there instead. It would also be a tiny monetary saving.

title: Feature: Proxy Support for aider
body:
### Issue

**Summary:**

This feature request proposes adding support for using proxies with Aider, the AI pair programming tool.

**Motivation:**

Currently, Aider directly connects to LLM APIs, which can be problematic in certain scenarios:

* **Network Restrictions:** Users behind firewalls or in environments with restricted internet access may be unable to directly connect to LLM APIs.
* **Privacy Concerns:** Some users may prefer routing their requests through a proxy for added privacy.

**Proposed Solution:**

Implement a configuration option within Aider to specify a proxy server address and port. Aider would then route all API requests through this proxy.

**Implementation Details:**

* **Configuration:**

title: Feature: pass context to lint-cmd commands on what changed
body:
# Problem

Today, when lint commands are run, they run over everything. This means that errors that have nothing to do with the changed code are given to the model, and the model is asked to take them into consideration. This means that asking for a minor change, may result in a massive change due to linting.

# Solution

Provide context as optional arguments to lint-cmd commands, perhaps using some sort of templating.

Information to pass:
- path to files effected
- line number ranges to files effected
- summary of changes (?)
- original request command (?)

This capability will allow the linting process to focus on relevant changes, reducing unnecessary token usage and minimizing confusion for the models by limiting the scope of linting to modified areas.

# Challenges

Most linting tools that I'm aware of don't actually allow specifying that only specific line ranges be covered. The solution to this will likely be wrapper scripts that take in the arguments and then filter out what is not needed. This should be left as an exercise to the user.

title: Feature Request: Configurable Command Prefix for LLM Interaction
body:
### Issue

I'm starting to use Aider and appreciate its integration into the development workflow. However, I've encountered an issue that could potentially improve the user experience and reduce token consumption errors.

### Issue Description

Currently, in Aider, commands for interacting with the LLM begin with a `/` prefix (e.g., `/add`, `/drop`). This system works well, but the default behavior allows any non-prefixed input to be sent directly to the LLM. This has led to several instances where I accidentally trigger the LLM because I forget to use the `/` prefix, leading to unnecessary token usage, especially in contexts with a large number of tokens.

### Suggested Feature

I propose adding a configuration option that changes the default interaction model with the LLM. Specifically, it would be beneficial to have a setting where:

- **Only commands prefixed with `/chat` are sent to the LLM**. This would prevent accidental activation of the LLM and help users manage token usage more efficiently.
- **Optionally, allow users to execute all commands without a prefix**, aligning more closely with typical terminal usage where commands are entered without a `/`.

This feature would help users like me, who spend significant time in the terminal, to adapt more seamlessly to Aider's command structure without frequent errors.

### Benefits

- **Reduces accidental LLM activations**: Limits unnecessary token loss and enhances user control.
- **Enhances user adaptation**: Aligns more closely with common terminal behaviors, easing the learning curve for new and transitioning users.

title: Aider .env precedence is wrong, does not behave as documented.
body:
### Issue

Aider does not load the correct `OPENAI_API_KEY`. I have it defined in both my home directory and my .git root (which also happens to be my current directory). 

### Expectation

Aider uses the `OPENAI_API_KEY` from my git root / current directory, not the one in my home directory.

### Behaviour

Aider is using the key that's specified in my home directory, this behaviour can also be seen if I set the key as a User or System environment variable, that defined env var will take precedence over .env files, which feels incorrect and also does not align with the documented behaviour.

### Documentation

https://aider.chat/docs/config.html#configuration
> Aider has many options which can be set with command line switches. Most options can also be set in an .aider.conf.yml file which can be placed in your home directory or at the root of your git repo. Or by setting environment variables like AIDER_xxx either in your shell or a .env file.

https://aider.chat/docs/config/dotenv.html#config-with-env
> Aider will look for a .env file in these locations:
> Your **home** directory.
> The **root** of your git repo.
> The **current** directory.
> As specified with the --env-file <filename> parameter.
> If the files above exist, they will be loaded in that order. **Files loaded last will take priority**.

### Hypothesis & Workarounds

I have not found a workaround to get hierarchical environment variables working. I tried using --env-file on the command line, and still the home dir env takes precedence. 

1. Initially I suspected that perhaps the OPENAI_API_KEY was already loaded into my shell, and Aider was letting the shell's environment take precedence over .env (behaviour I would still find confusing). However, I have verified that this is not the case. OPENAI_API_KEY is not defined in the shell before launching Aider.
2. I can confirm that if I define OPENAI_API_KEY on the CLI before launching Aider, that value takes precedence. 
3. I can confirm that if I use --openai-api-key on the CLI, that has the highest precedence. 

Thus, the behaviour seems to match ConfigArgParse of command line > environment variables > config file values > defaults, where environment variables are trampling .env files. 

What I do not expect, is that `~/.env` is being loaded between the launch of Aider and the ConfigArgParse, populating the environment and causing the config file values to not work as expected. 

I have tried using AIDER_OPENAI_API_KEY to see if that auto loads in ConfigArgParse and tramples the environment, that does not work either.

I see python-dotenv is a transient dependency of lite-llm, but that should have behaviour that works in my favour, not against it. 

```
python-dotenv==1.0.1
    # via litellm
```

### Screenshot

I echo the API key via /run to demonstrate that the environment is not populated correctly, when Aider tries to make a commit in this configuration (because its using GPT-3.5 as weak model) it will fail as it will use 'homedir' as the API key instead of the correct key defined in my project.

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c12cc39b-b634-46fe-ac80-b1a195fb6121)

Aider v0.43.4
Model: claude-3.5-sonnet / gpt-3.5-turbo
Git repo: 497 files
Repo-map 1024

title: Enhancement: Only commit staged files if files have been staged.
body:
### Issue

I appreciate Aider's commit messages; they often surpass Copilot's, which seems to have declined recently.

In my workflow, I stage the files I intend to commit, create a commit message for them, and then proceed to stage the next set of files. 

I'm considering using Aider's `/commit` feature for this process. However, Aider currently stages and commits all modified files.

This doesn't align with my method of working alongside Aider, where I prefer to commit only the staged files, not every changed file.

Additionally, I've observed that Aider overlooks new files during `/commit`. If `/commit` is designed to stage and commit all changes, excluding new files appears to be an oversight.

title: Improve user input formatting in `--chat-history-file`
body:
## Current Behavior

The `--chat-history-file` option in Aider creates a markdown file to store chat history. However, the current implementation uses level 4 headings (`####`) to prefix user input entries in the chat history. This formatting is not ideal for the content being stored.

## Proposed Change

Replace the use of headings (`####`) with blockquotes (`>`) for user input entries in the chat history. This change would better represent the nature of the content and improve readability of the chat history file.

## Rationale

1. Headings are typically used for structuring document content, not for representing user inputs in a chat-like format.
2. Blockquotes are more semantically appropriate for representing user inputs in a chat history.
3. This change will make the user input sections in the chat history file more consistent with common markdown usage patterns.

## Current Implementation

The [relevant code in the `user_input` method](https://github.com/paul-gauthier/aider/blob/5ae96231ad5be9158e35bb916b3d276f3139d18a/aider/io.py#L304-L319):

```python
prefix = "####"
if inp:
    hist = inp.splitlines()
else:
    hist = ["<blank>"]

hist = f"  \n{prefix} ".join(hist)

hist = f"""
{prefix} {hist}"""
self.append_chat_history(hist, linebreak=True)
```

## Suggested Implementation
Replace `prefix = "####"` with `prefix = ">"` and adjust the formatting accordingly:

```python
prefix = ">"
if inp:
    hist = inp.splitlines()
else:
    hist = ["<blank>"]

hist = f"\n{prefix} ".join(hist)

hist = f"""
{prefix} {hist}"""
self.append_chat_history(hist, linebreak=True)
```

This change will format each line of the user input as a separate blockquote, which is more appropriate for chat-like content.

title: Request: allow attachment of external files for inclusion in requests
body:
**The issue**

Just like the 'coding conventions' example in the docs, including extra structured context data (aside from the codemaps aider auto generates) is really useful.  That example is static though - there are lots of examples where the extra files must update each request:

- updated screenshots of the webpage, app or whatever.  
- In some tools important info is in binary or weird xml files and won't be in aider's codemap.  eg. I have a Unity script that creates a nice text file of object hierarchy and each object's properties.

Given it's static and must be in git, I'd have to do this each request:

1. Take the screenshot, into project folder (or run dump, whatever)
2. Do a git commit
3. /drop the old image/text file
4. /add the new image/text file. 
5. Make the request

**Proposal**
An '/attach' command ie. '/attach mypropertymap.txt' (or myimage.png)

- Attached files differ from files we /add.  They aren't 'in the project and editable by aider', they are read only, and solely get sent up to the model for context.  This means they don't have to be in git, it's a normal filepath anywhere on my file system.
- They are freshly loaded from the filesystem each time aider does a request.  This lets the user have their own workflow for autoscreenshotting their app, updating their dump files every 10 seconds, etc.

A /detach command would go alongside it, so these reference files can persist through your normal workflow as you separately add and drop 'aider managed' files.

This would be powerful I think!  The /web command may already have implemented much of what's needed - a read only addition to context which aider knows it doesn't edit.  I'm not sure if you can remove things added with /web so perhaps it would become /attachweb to make it clear you can /detach web files too.

Ideally the name of the attached file would go up so you can say in the aider request 'refer to the attached blah.txt file' and the model knows what file name/content that is.

Thanks for listening Paul!

title: [FeatReq] Add support for apps and libs that require two console to develop (like Textual)
body:
### Issue

Certain python apps and libraries require multiple terminal consoles open at the same time.
This is because the TUI interface is displayed in one console, while the debug messages are displayed in another console.
Textual is an example. [Textual](https://github.com/Textualize/textual) is the most popular TUI framework for Python, used to develop apps like [Elia](https://github.com/darrenburns/elia), [Memray](https://github.com/bloomberg/memray), [Parllama](https://github.com/paulrobello/parllama) and [Posting](https://github.com/darrenburns/posting).
The dev mode of Textual requires some special setup on two consoles. You can read about it here:

https://textual.textualize.io/guide/devtools/
https://github.com/Textualize/textual-dev

Currently Aider cannot monitor or display two consoles at the same time, and consequently developing Textual apps with it is impossible. Because the AI needs both the console outputs (the debug logs messages and the TUI snapshots) added to the chat to understand what is going on. This is also somewhat related to this issue: https://github.com/paul-gauthier/aider/issues/912 .
Please add support for displaying and adding to chat multiple consoles output. 

P.S.
Writing tests for Textual is also difficult for the same reason. But you can use a tool like `pytest-textual-snapshot` to handle those UI tests in Aider once you implement the dual console output. Please add support for it. You can read about it here:

https://textual.textualize.io/guide/testing/
https://github.com/Textualize/pytest-textual-snapshot

Thanks! 😊 🙏

title: Add option to resize images to reduce API costs
body:
### Issue

# Background
Currently, when using image-capable LLM providers, the cost is usually based on the dimensions of the uploaded images. However, many screenshots or photos contain information that is still visible and useful at much smaller sizes.

# Feature Request
Add a command-line option to aider that allows users to set a maximum size for images. This would involve resizing images before sending them to the LLM provider, potentially significantly reducing costs without losing essential information.

# Proposed Implementation
1. Add a new command-line parameter, e.g., `--max-image-size 1024x768`
2. Implement an image resizing function that:
   - Checks the dimensions of input images
   - Resizes images that exceed the specified maximum size while maintaining aspect ratio
   - Uses a high-quality resizing algorithm to preserve image clarity

# Benefits
- Reduced API costs for users
- Faster upload times for large images
- Potentially faster processing times from the LLM provider

# Considerations
- The resizing should be optional and off by default to maintain backward compatibility
- Users should be warned if they're uploading large images without this option enabled
- Consider adding options for different resizing algorithms or quality settings

# Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] New command-line parameter added and documented
- [ ] Image resizing function implemented and tested
- [ ] Warning system for large images implemented
- [ ] Performance impact of resizing measured and documented

# Additional Notes
This feature would be particularly useful for users who frequently work with screenshots or other large images that don't require full resolution for LLM analysis.
